entry.evidence: there are still no thermal EoS studies of Cr-pyrope at high P–T

steps.action: The authors pose the problem: the thermal EoS of Cr-pyrope, needed for elastic geobarometry of diamond inclusions, is missing, and its compositional dependence is uninvestigated.
steps.quote: there are still no thermal EoS studies of Cr-pyrope at high P–T

steps.action: They cite the common assumption that the solid-solution bulk modulus mixes linearly from end members (a Vegard analogue), and the rival reports of nonlinear dependence for grossular-bearing solutions.
steps.quote: the bulk modulus of garnet solid solution is often considered to be calculated from the bulk moduli of its end members

steps.action: They design a synchrotron SCXRD study at high P, high T and high P–T on five natural Cr-pyropes spanning Cr2O3 0.1–7.3 wt.% to extract complete thermal EoS parameters and their compositional effects.
steps.quote: single-crystal X-ray difraction (SCXRD) measurements on

steps.action: They characterize the Zhenyuan lamproite garnets by EMPA (end-member proportions after Locock 2008, Fe3+ by charge balance) and BSE imaging, and check that the samples are unzoned and resemble diamond-inclusion compositions.
steps.quote: (BSE) images reveal that these garnets are not zoned into

steps.action: They set the P–T conditions in three runs: room-T high-P to 9.5 GPa (BX90 DAC, neon medium, gold pressure scale), resistively heated DAC to 13 GPa and 700 K, and room-P capillary heating to 950 K.
steps.quote: Three runs of SCXRD experiments were conducted for these Cr-pyropes.

steps.action: They collect diffraction images at APS 13-BM-D and 13-BM-C (LaB6 standard; ATREX and APEX3 processing), obtain unit-cell volumes, and observe a smooth compression with no phase transition.
steps.quote: The obtained unit-cell parameters of each Cr-pyrope are shown in Table S2.

steps.action: They fit the room-T P–V data with a BM3 EoS in EosFit7 to estimate VT0, KT0 and K′T0 with uncertainties.
steps.quote: we ft the P–V data to a third-order Birch–Murnaghan

steps.action: They refit the P–V data with a third-order Tait EoS and check the BM3 fit with fE–FE plots; both agree with the BM3 parameters (K′ near 4, except Prp-Cr#22.4 above 4).
steps.quote: Tait EoS and BM3 EoS ftting yield indistinguishable EoS parameters within the uncertainty

steps.action: They fit the P–V–T data with an isothermal BM3 + Fei thermal-expansion model with a constant (∂KT/∂T)P, holding the room-T parameters fixed, to estimate α0, α1, α2 and (∂KT/∂T)P.
steps.quote: We used an isothermal EoS model (Text S1) to ft the P–V–T data

steps.action: They replace the constant (∂KT/∂T)P with the Helffrich and Connolly (2009) Anderson–Grüneisen formulation and find nearly identical thermal parameters.
steps.quote: using the HC2009 equation did not yield much diference in the EoS parameters

steps.action: They fit the data with the Holland and Powell (2011) thermal-pressure EoS (Einstein temperature 508–522 K) as an alternative model and report good fits and α300 values.
steps.quote: showing good EoS ft for each Cr-pyrope

steps.action: They compare the five samples: KT0 differs by at most 2.8%, and the high K′T0 of Prp-Cr#22.4 is attributed to its knorringite component.
steps.quote: the compositional efects are very limited for

steps.action: They check their KT0 against the independent RPR measurements on Cr-pyropes by Babuška et al. (1978) and find agreement.
steps.quote: are comparable to the KT0 of Cr-pyropes

steps.action: They compile literature KT0 values for Prp, Alm, Grs and Uvr end members, favour direct measurements, and compare compression curves with the Cr-pyropes.
steps.quote: As shown in Fig. 4, Alm100 is the least compressible and Uvr100 is the most compressible.

steps.action: They compare room-P thermal expansion and α300 of the Cr-pyropes with literature end-member values and find the Cr-pyropes expand more than room-P high-T XRD end members.
steps.quote: the fve Cr-pyropes have larger

steps.action: They compare the high P–T data with end-member high P–T EoS (Fig. 7a–d; VT/VT0 at 10 GPa, Fig. 5b) and find comparable expansivities to Prp and Alm and higher ones than Grs and Uvr.
steps.quote: at high P, the thermal expansivities of Prp-Cr#0.3 and Prp-Cr#4.4 are higher than that of Prp100

steps.action: They compute ideal (Vegard) end-member mixing volumes at high P–T from published end-member EoS and the measured compositions, excluding minor end members and Prp-Cr#22.4.
steps.quote: to calculate the end-member volumes at high P–T

steps.action: They compare the measured EoS with the mixing model: VT0 is larger (positive excess volume), but after a VT0 correction the volumes agree within about 0.2%.
steps.quote: After the discrepancy in VT0 is corrected, the EoS of Cr-pyrope predicts much more consistent values with the end-member mixing model.

steps.action: They reject the reading that the higher expansivities indicate large excess thermal expansivity, attributing the gap to room-P versus high P–T XRD differences in the literature.
steps.quote: the excess thermal expansivity in Cr-pyrope, if any, should be rather small

steps.action: They compare (∂KT/∂T)P of the Cr-pyropes with end-member literature values (Prp, Grs and Uvr near -0.02 GPa/K; Alm -0.043 GPa/K).
steps.quote: Prp-Cr#0.3 is closer to the Alm100 trend

steps.action: They check the fitted (∂KT/∂T)P against the independent RPR high-T elasticity of a similar natural Cr-pyrope (Suzuki and Anderson 1983) and find agreement.
steps.quote: yielded comparable values of (∂KT/∂T)P to that obtained by direct measurement of elasticity

steps.action: They summarize the retained parameter results: KT0 within 3% of Prp100; expansivity larger than room-P but comparable to high P–T end-member data; (∂KT/∂T)P close to Prp, Grs and Uvr.
steps.quote: To summarize, the results of this study indicate that

steps.action: They compute entrapment-pressure isomekes with EosFit-Pinc for the five Cr-pyropes and for the end members (both room-P and high P–T expansivity sets), assuming Pi = 0.2 GPa and the diamond EoS of Angel et al. (2015).
steps.quote: assume Pi=0.2 GPa which could be for garnet inclusion in peridotitic diamond

steps.action: They compare the Pe curves across the Cr-pyropes: Pe groups follow thermal-expansion groups, so expansivity rather than compressibility controls the calculated Pe.
steps.quote: the variation in thermal expansion behavior plays a more signifcant role

steps.action: They compare the Cr-pyrope Pe with end-member Pe: it agrees better with high P–T based values; low-Cr samples sit near pyrope and high-Cr samples near grossular and uvarovite.
steps.quote: Prp-Cr#0.3 and Prp-Cr#4.4 have very close Pe to Prp100

end.claim: Five natural Cr-pyropes (Cr# 0.3–22.4) have thermal EoS parameters (KT0 165.4–170.2 GPa, α300 2.73–2.96 ×10−5 K−1, (∂KT/∂T)P −0.031 to −0.019 GPa/K) whose thermal expansivity varies up to 8.8% while compressibility varies at most 2.8%, so expansivity controls the calculated diamond-inclusion Pe.

decisive_move.sentence: Fitting the in situ SCXRD P–V–T data of the five Cr-pyropes to a BM3 + Fei thermal EoS produced the parameters on which every comparison and Pe calculation rests.

gates.evidence: Data acquisition was directed by a gap (missing thermal EoS; untested compositional effects), not by a stated hypothesis (p. 2). The estimates faced checks they could have failed: alternative EoS forms (p. 4), the independent RPR values of Babuška et al. 1978 (p. 6) and Suzuki and Anderson 1983 (p. 12), and the ideal-mixing comparison (p. 11). The Pe application assumes a hypothetical Pi and is not tested against measured inclusions. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgements name an editor and two reviewers, but no changes they caused can be coded. Composition is none_fits: this is a measurement-and-estimation campaign without stated rivals tested by a crucial experiment, apart from a weak ideal-mixing comparison. Sub-claims: 'excess thermal expansivity, if any, is small' is a best_explanation, resting on literature differences between room-P and high P–T XRD and a 0.2% model discrepancy (p. 11). 'Thermal expansion dominates Pe' and 'low-Cr near pyrope, high-Cr near grossular' are simulation-based comparisons under an assumed Pi = 0.2 GPa, with no measured inclusions (pp. 12-13); their status is best_explanation at most. Inference: the Holland–Powell α300 values (2.568–2.908) are systematically lower than the isothermal-model values (2.73–2.96) for the high-Cr samples, and the paper does not discuss this. The samples are lamproite garnets, not actual inclusions. Minor reporting inconsistencies: 'Prp-Cr#3.5' on p. 3, and Table 3 footnote labels for Prp-Cr#22.4 (p. 8). Choices reported without alternatives: fixing the room-T parameters during thermal fits, the diamond EoS, and Pi.

disagreements.target: Room-P high-T XRD thermal expansivities of end-member garnets (Milani et al. 2015, 2017; Skinner 1956; Thieblot et al. 1998)
disagreements.support: These values are much lower than the high P–T XRD values. The Cr-pyropes agree with the latter, so the apparent excess expansivity reflects the end-member data source.
disagreements.quote: reported much lower thermal expansivities for Prp100, Alm100, and Grs100
